knitr::opts_chunk$set(

library(tidyverse)

# 1. Introduction

This R Markdown document presents the Logistic Regression model used to predict customer recommendation behaviour for Gelugor Fashion Store. The target variable is `recommend_index`, where customers are classified as either `Recommend` or `Not_Recommend`. The `Not_Recommend` class is treated as the positive class in the confusion matrix because it represents loyalty-risk customers who may require targeted improvement actions.

# 2. Load Dataset

```{r load-data}
final_ml_dataset <- read_csv("final_ml_dataset.csv")

dim(final_ml_dataset)
str(final_ml_dataset)
summary(final_ml_dataset)
head(final_ml_dataset)
```

## Target Distribution Before Conversion

```{r target-before-conversion}
table(final_ml_dataset$recommend_index)
prop.table(table(final_ml_dataset$recommend_index))
```

# 3. Convert Target Variable

The target variable is converted from `0` and `1` into meaningful labels. A value of `0` represents `Not_Recommend`, while a value of `1` represents `Recommend`.

```{r convert-target}
final_ml_dataset$recommend_index <- factor(
  as.character(final_ml_dataset$recommend_index),
  levels = c("0", "1"),
  labels = c("Not_Recommend", "Recommend")
)

table(final_ml_dataset$recommend_index)
prop.table(table(final_ml_dataset$recommend_index))
str(final_ml_dataset$recommend_index)
```

# 4. Data Type Preparation

Character predictors are converted into factors so that they can be used properly in the Logistic Regression model.

```{r data-type-preparation}
final_ml_dataset <- final_ml_dataset %>%
  mutate(
    across(where(is.character), as.factor)
  )

str(final_ml_dataset)
```

# 5. Stratified Train-Test Split

The dataset is split into 70% training data and 30% testing data using stratified sampling. This helps maintain the proportion of `Recommend` and `Not_Recommend` customers in both the training and testing sets.

```{r train-test-split}
set.seed(123)

sample_index <- createDataPartition(
  final_ml_dataset$recommend_index,
  p = 0.7,
  list = FALSE
)

train_data <- final_ml_dataset[sample_index, ]
test_data  <- final_ml_dataset[-sample_index, ]

dim(train_data)
dim(test_data)

table(train_data$recommend_index)
table(test_data$recommend_index)
```

# 6. Build Logistic Regression Model

Logistic Regression is used because the target variable is binary. The model estimates the probability that a customer belongs to the `Recommend` class.

```{r build-logistic-model}
logit_model <- glm(
  recommend_index ~ .,
  data = train_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(logit_model)
```

# 7. Predict Probabilities and Classes

The model predicts the probability of a customer being classified as `Recommend`. A threshold of 0.5 is used to convert predicted probabilities into class labels.

```{r prediction}
pred_prob <- predict(
  logit_model,
  newdata = test_data,
  type = "response"
)

head(pred_prob)

pred_class <- ifelse(
  pred_prob > 0.5,
  "Recommend",
  "Not_Recommend"
)

pred_class <- factor(
  pred_class,
  levels = c("Not_Recommend", "Recommend")
)

test_data$recommend_index <- factor(
  test_data$recommend_index,
  levels = c("Not_Recommend", "Recommend")
)

head(pred_class)
```

# 8. Confusion Matrix

The confusion matrix evaluates how many customers were correctly and incorrectly classified. The positive class is set as `Not_Recommend` because this group represents loyalty-risk customers.

```{r confusion-matrix}
conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(
  data = pred_class,
  reference = test_data$recommend_index,
  positive = "Not_Recommend"
)

conf_matrix
```

## Key Classification Metrics

```{r key-metrics}
accuracy  <- conf_matrix$overall["Accuracy"]
precision <- conf_matrix$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]
recall    <- conf_matrix$byClass["Sensitivity"]

f1_score <- 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall)

accuracy
precision
recall
f1_score
```

## Save Confusion Matrix Table

```{r save-confusion-matrix-table}
logit_cm_table <- as.data.frame(conf_matrix$table)

logit_cm_table

write_csv(logit_cm_table, "LogisticRegression_ConfusionMatrix_Table.csv")
```

## Confusion Matrix Heatmap

```{r confusion-matrix-plot}
logit_cm_plot <- ggplot(logit_cm_table, aes(x = Reference, y = Prediction, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = Freq,
      colour = ifelse(Freq > max(Freq) / 2, "white", "black")
    ),
    size = 6
  ) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#DEEBF7",
    high = "#3182BD"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Logistic Regression Confusion Matrix",
    x = "Actual Class",
    y = "Predicted Class",
    fill = "Freq"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 13),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11)
  )

logit_cm_plot

ggsave(
  "LogisticRegression_ConfusionMatrix.png",
  logit_cm_plot,
  width = 6,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)
```

# 9. Feature Importance Using Coefficients

The coefficients of the Logistic Regression model show the direction and strength of each predictor. Positive coefficients increase the probability of the `Recommend` class, while negative coefficients decrease it.

```{r coefficients}
logit_coef <- coef(logit_model)

logit_coef
```

## Coefficient Table

```{r coefficient-table}
coef_table <- data.frame(
  Feature = names(logit_coef),
  Coefficient = as.numeric(logit_coef)
) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(Coefficient)))

coef_table

write_csv(coef_table, "LogisticRegression_Coefficients.csv")
```

## Top Coefficient Plot

```{r coefficient-plot}
top_coef <- coef_table %>%
  filter(Feature != "(Intercept)") %>%
  slice_max(order_by = abs(Coefficient), n = 15)

coef_plot <- ggplot(
  top_coef,
  aes(x = reorder(Feature, Coefficient), y = Coefficient)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 15 Logistic Regression Coefficients",
    x = "Feature",
    y = "Coefficient"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

coef_plot

ggsave(
  "LogisticRegression_Coefficients.png",
  coef_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)
```

# 10. ROC Curve and AUC

The ROC curve evaluates the model's ability to separate `Recommend` and `Not_Recommend` customers. A higher AUC value indicates stronger classification separability.

```{r roc-auc}
roc_logit <- roc(
  response = test_data$recommend_index,
  predictor = pred_prob,
  levels = c("Not_Recommend", "Recommend"),
  direction = "<"
)

auc_value <- auc(roc_logit)

auc_value
```

## ROC Curve Plot

```{r roc-plot}
plot(
  roc_logit,
  col = "blue",
  main = paste0(
    "Logistic Regression ROC Curve (AUC = ",
    round(auc_value, 3),
    ")"
  )
)

png("LogisticRegression_ROC.png", width = 1000, height = 800, res = 150)

plot(
  roc_logit,
  col = "blue",
  main = paste0(
    "Logistic Regression ROC Curve (AUC = ",
    round(auc_value, 3),
    ")"
  )
)

dev.off()
```

# 11. Save Logistic Regression Performance Metrics

The model performance is summarized using Accuracy, Kappa, Balanced Accuracy, Recall, Specificity, Precision, F1-score and AUC. Since the business objective focuses on detecting loyalty-risk customers, Recall for `Not_Recommend` and Balanced Accuracy are important evaluation metrics.

```{r save-metrics}
logit_metrics <- data.frame(
  Model = "Logistic Regression",
  Accuracy = as.numeric(conf_matrix$overall["Accuracy"]),
  Kappa = as.numeric(conf_matrix$overall["Kappa"]),
  Balanced_Accuracy = as.numeric(conf_matrix$byClass["Balanced Accuracy"]),
  Recall_NotRecommend = as.numeric(conf_matrix$byClass["Sensitivity"]),
  Specificity_Recommend = as.numeric(conf_matrix$byClass["Specificity"]),
  Precision_NotRecommend = as.numeric(conf_matrix$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]),
  F1_NotRecommend = as.numeric(conf_matrix$byClass["F1"]),
  AUC = as.numeric(auc_value)
)

logit_metrics

write_csv(logit_metrics, "LogisticRegression_Metrics.csv")
```

# 12. Save Final Model

The final Logistic Regression model is saved as an RDS file so that it can be reused later for prediction or model deployment.

```{r save-model}
saveRDS(logit_model, "LogisticRegression_Model.rds")
```

# 13. Conclusion

The Logistic Regression model was developed to predict whether customers would recommend a clothing item. It is useful because it provides both classification results and interpretable coefficients. The model can identify how product, customer, rating, review engagement and review-text features influence the probability of recommendation. Since `Not_Recommend` customers represent loyalty-risk customers, the model is especially useful when it achieves strong Recall for `Not_Recommend`, Balanced Accuracy and AUC.
